title: Review: Statistical tests; Circulatory systems and blood vessels; Haemoglobin and oxygen transport
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PR03b#t1 term and clue written for the game; EX05#t4 term and clue written for the game; PR03b#t4 term and clue written for the game; EX05#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EX05#N.8, EX09#N.9, PR03b#N.9, EX05#N.18, EX09#N.4, PR03b#N.7, EX05#N.11, EX09#N.7, EX09#N.14. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Student's t-test
items.clue: Used to compare two means of continuous data that are roughly normally distributed.

items.label: Capillaries
items.clue: Narrow vessels with a wall one cell thick, where flow is slowest and exchange occurs

items.label: Critical value
items.clue: Number at p = 0.05 that t must equal or exceed for the difference to be significant.

items.label: Mass transport
items.clue: Flow of a whole fluid, driven by a pump, moving substances quickly over large distances

questions.stem: What is the role of the elastic tissue in the wall of an artery?

options.text: It contracts in waves behind the blood to push it along the artery towards the tissues.
It makes the wall stiff and rigid so that the high pressure cannot burst the artery.
It stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, maintaining pressure.
It forms flaps that actively open and shut to push blood forwards along the artery.

questions.explanation: Stretching during ventricular contraction stores energy; recoil returns it while the ventricle relaxes, keeping blood moving and pressure high between beats.

questions.stem: In the placenta, maternal blood and foetal blood are separated by a thin barrier. How is oxygen transferred from maternal blood to foetal blood?

options.text: Foetal haemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen, so that it releases oxygen to the rapidly growing foetal tissues more easily than adult haemoglobin would.
Maternal red blood cells pass across the barrier into the foetal circulation and deliver their oxygen directly to the foetus.
Maternal haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen rises in the placenta because the foetus needs oxygen, so it hands its oxygen on to the foetus.
Foetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen, so at the oxygen concentration in the placenta it loads oxygen that maternal haemoglobin releases.

questions.stem: A student counts the heart rate of Daphnia in pond water (control) and in a caffeine solution, 10 Daphnia in each. - Control: mean 212 beats per minute, SD 18. - Caffeine: mean 231 beats per minute, SD 20. Critical values of t at p = 0.05: 9 degrees of freedom, 2.26; 18, 2.10; 20, 2.09. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: t = 9.75, far above 2.10, so the difference is highly significant.
t = 2.23, above 2.10 for 18 degrees of freedom, so reject the null hypothesis.
t = 2.23, below 2.26 for 9 degrees of freedom, so accept the null hypothesis.
t = 2.23, above 2.10, which proves caffeine raises the heart rate of every Daphnia.

questions.stem: With age, the walls of large arteries lose elastic tissue and become stiffer. Blood pressure in an arm artery is measured at its highest (as the ventricle contracts) and its lowest (between beats). What change in these readings is expected?

options.text: The readings become steadier, because a stiff wall resists the surges better than a stretchy one.
The highest reading rises and the lowest falls: the swing in pressure gets bigger.
The lowest reading falls to zero, because nothing keeps blood under pressure between beats.
No change, because the muscle in the artery wall contracts with each beat to keep the pressure steady.

questions.stem: Adult haemoglobin is about 20% saturated with oxygen at a partial pressure of oxygen of 2 kPa, 60% at 4 kPa, 90% at 8 kPa and 98% at 13 kPa. Which explanation accounts for this pattern?

options.text: The four haem groups fill one after another at equal rates, so saturation rises in direct proportion to the oxygen concentration.
The curve shows the order in which haemoglobin loads over time, from its arrival in the lungs to full saturation.
Saturation rises steeply from 2 to 8 kPa because each oxygen bound raises the affinity of the other haem groups.
The plateau above 8 kPa is where haemoglobin releases most of its oxygen to tissues, because saturation is highest there.

questions.stem: For 10 quadrats, a student ranks the density of a moss and the soil moisture content, and finds Σd² = 60. The critical value of rₛ for n = 10 at p = 0.05 is 0.648. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: rₛ = 0.64, which is below 0.648, so there is no significant correlation.
rₛ = 0.36, a weak positive correlation that is not significant.
rₛ = 0.64, a positive value, so there is a significant positive correlation.
rₛ = 0.64, which is greater than 0.05, so the correlation is significant.

questions.explanation: rₛ = 1 − (6 × 60) ÷ (10 × 99) = 1 − 360 ÷ 990 = 0.64. Just below the critical value: the correlation could be due to chance.

questions.stem: A muscle receives blood through a network of thousands of capillaries rather than through a single vessel of the same total volume. What is the advantage of this arrangement for exchange?

options.text: A single wide vessel would have more wall area than thousands of narrow ones, so exchange inside it would be faster.
The narrow capillaries force the blood through faster, so more oxygen is delivered to the muscle each second.
Each capillary has fenestrations, which are needed so that cells can pass out of the blood into the muscle.
The total surface area of the many narrow, branching vessels is far larger, and all the blood is close to a wall.

questions.stem: Blood leaves the lungs at pH 7.4, 98% saturated. In a working muscle, pO₂ is 4 kPa and the extra CO₂ has lowered the pH to 7.2. At 4 kPa, saturation is 57% at pH 7.4 and 43% at pH 7.2. By how many percentage points does the saturation of this blood fall in the muscle?
questions.explanation: 98 − 43 = 55 percentage points. The Bohr effect adds 14 points to what low pO₂ alone would release (41).

questions.stem: As blood flows through the lung capillaries, CO₂ diffuses out of it into the alveoli. How does this help the blood load oxygen?

options.text: Haemoglobin's affinity for O₂ rises, so it loads O₂ more fully at the lungs' pO₂.
The curve shifts right, so haemoglobin's affinity rises and it loads more O₂.
Nothing changes, because only the high pO₂ in the lungs affects loading.
CO₂ leaving frees the haem groups it was blocking, so O₂ can bind to them.

questions.explanation: Less CO₂ (and higher pH) shifts the curve left. Higher affinity means fuller loading in the lungs.
